Certainly! A Q-Q (Quantile-Quantile) plot is a graphical tool used in statistics to compare two probability distributions. In the context of regression analysis, it's often used to check if residuals (the differences between observed and predicted values) follow a normal distribution.

Imagine you have a set of data points that come from an unknown distribution. The goal is to see how well your model fits this data. To do this, we can simulate new data sets under different assumptions about the distribution and then plot these simulated data against our actual data on a Q-Q plot.

If the residuals (the difference between each observed value and its corresponding fitted value) come from a normally distributed population, they should roughly lie along a straight line when plotted against their quantiles (or percentiles). This straight line would represent perfect fit since all data points should fall exactly on it if the assumption holds true.

In summary, a Q-Q plot helps us determine whether our model’s residuals are randomly distributed or if there might be some systematic deviations from what we expect from a random sample drawn from a normal distribution.
